item.title: Syllabus (Postgraduate)
item.description:
Introduction to Second Language Acquisition (Postgraduate) #

Note: This syllabus outlines the plan for a 12-week, seminar-style course. Minor adjustments may be made as we progress.

Course Description #

This graduate seminar is a research-oriented introduction to how adults acquire second and additional languages. We emphasize linguistic architecture, cross-linguistic variation, interfaces, processing, and implications for teaching, using Slabakova (2016) as the anchor text. Part I establishes language architecture and variation; Part II situates L2 within broader acquisition contexts and highlights the role of input; Part III surveys adult L2 morphology, syntax, the mental lexicon, interfaces, processing, and classroom implications.

item.title: Week 1 — Language Architecture & SLA as a Science
item.description:
Week 1 — Language Architecture & SLA as a Science #

Anchor text: Slabakova, R. (2016). Second Language Acquisition. Chapter 1: Language architecture.

⭐ Overview (for preview) #

  • What it means to “know” a language and how this knowledge is structured into interacting modules.
  • How SLA research adopts the scientific method: observe → generalize → hypothesize → test → revise.
  • Why theory should make predictions (e.g., rich agreement → possible null subjects) and be falsifiable.
  • How “teaching relevance” follows from language architecture (different modules can pose different difficulties).

🎯 Learning goals #

By the end of Week 1 you should be able to:

item.title: Week 2 — Language Variation & the Learning Task
item.description:
Week 2 — Language Variation & the Learning Task #

Anchor text: Slabakova (2016), Second Language Acquisition, Chapter 2.

⭐ Overview (for preview) #

  • How languages can differ (word order, agreement, null subjects, verb movement), and what exactly an L2 learner must acquire.
  • Principles & Parameters / Minimalist ideas: what is fixed vs. what varies; the role of features.
  • The learning task: initial state, transfer, input “triggers,” and how learners re-set feature values.

🎯 Learning goals #

By the end of this week you should be able to:

item.title: Week 3 — Processing & the Parser: How L2 is Used in Real Time
item.description:
Week 3 — Processing & the Parser: How L2 is Used in Real Time #

Anchor text: Slabakova (2016), Second Language Acquisition, Chapter 3.

⭐ Overview (for preview) #

  • How the mind parses language incrementally and what this implies for second language (L2) comprehension and production.
  • Core processing architectures and why performance sometimes diverges from grammatical competence.
  • What L2 processing predicts for error signatures, reaction times, and eye-movement patterns, and how methods can detect them.

🎯 Learning goals #

By the end of this week you should be able to:

item.title: Week 4 — Age, Input & the Critical Period
item.description:
Week 4 — Age, Input & the Critical Period #

Anchor text: Slabakova (2016), Second Language Acquisition, Chapter 4.

⭐ Overview (for preview) #

  • What Critical/Sensitive Period claims predict for L2 acquisition and how these claims are tested.
  • How input quantity and quality shape outcomes — sometimes more than age — and how to disentangle their effects.
  • Why conclusions hinge on measurement choices (global accent vs. fine-grained morphosyntax) and design controls (AoA, LoR, education, use, dominance).

🎯 Learning goals #

By the end of this week you should be able to:

item.title: Week 5 — Comparing Acquisition Contexts: 2L1, Adult L2, Heritage & Attrition
item.description:
Week 5 — Comparing Acquisition Contexts: 2L1, Adult L2, Heritage & Attrition #

Anchor text: Slabakova (2016), Second Language Acquisition, Ch. 5–6 (selected).

⭐ Overview (for preview) #

  • How acquisition context (simultaneous bilingualism/2L1, sequential/Adult L2, Heritage, Attrition) shapes the path and outcomes of acquisition.
  • What transfers, what restructures, and how input timing/amount/quality and dominance shift predictions.
  • Practical takeaways for designing studies and targeted instruction in each group.

🎯 Learning goals #

By the end of this week you should be able to:

item.title: Week 6 — Functional Morphology: Where (and Why) L2 Morphology Is Fragile
item.description:
Week 6 — Functional Morphology: Where (and Why) L2 Morphology Is Fragile #

Anchor text: Slabakova (2016), Second Language Acquisition, Chapter 7.

⭐ Overview (for preview) #

  • Why inflectional morphology (tense, agreement, case, gender) is often the locus of difficulty in L2 and heritage grammars.
  • Competing explanations: representation (features not fully acquired/reassembled) vs. performance (surface realization problems, prosodic/mapping issues).
  • Practical tools to test these views with targeted contrasts and diagnostic tasks.

🎯 Learning goals #

By the end of this week you should be able to:

item.title: Week 7 — Syntax: Word Order, Movement, and Competing Accounts
item.description:
Week 7 — Syntax: Word Order, Movement, and Competing Accounts #

Anchor text: Slabakova (2016), Second Language Acquisition, Chapter 8.

⭐ Overview (for preview) #

  • How syntactic movement and word-order properties (e.g., V-to-T, V2, head direction) create specific challenges in L2 acquisition.
  • What long-distance dependencies (wh-movement, relative clauses, islands) reveal about L2 grammatical representations.
  • How to adjudicate between representational accounts (e.g., failed/feature deficits, full transfer/full access) and processing accounts (e.g., shallow structure under time pressure).

🎯 Learning goals #

By the end of this week you should be able to:

item.title: Week 8 — The Mental Lexicon: Representation, Access, and Argument Structure
item.description:
Week 8 — The Mental Lexicon: Representation, Access, and Argument Structure #

Anchor text: Slabakova (2016), Second Language Acquisition, Chapter 9.

⭐ Overview (for preview) #

  • How the bilingual mental lexicon is organized and accessed in real time: cross-language activation, inhibition, cognate/false-friend effects.
  • What L2 learners must acquire beyond word form and core meaning: feature bundles, morphological decomposition, collocations, and argument-structure mappings.
  • How to test lexical representation and access with lexical decision, (masked) priming, picture naming, and eye-tracking/ERP.

🎯 Learning goals #

By the end of this week you should be able to:

item.title: Week 9 — Syntax–Semantics Interface: Meaning Composition, Telicity, and Scope
item.description:
Week 9 — Syntax–Semantics Interface: Meaning Composition, Telicity, and Scope #

Anchor text: Slabakova (2016), Second Language Acquisition, Chapter 10.

⭐ Overview (for preview) #

  • How syntactic structure and semantic composition interact to yield meanings (event types, definiteness/specificity, scope).
  • Why L2 learners struggle with telicity/aspect, article semantics, and quantifier scope—and what this predicts for data patterns.
  • Minimal, testable designs for the interface: truth-value judgment, acceptability with controlled contexts, and online measures.

🎯 Learning goals #

By the end of this week you should be able to:

item.title: Week 10 — Syntax–Discourse & Semantics–Pragmatics Interfaces
item.description:
Week 10 — Syntax–Discourse & Semantics–Pragmatics Interfaces #

Anchor text: Slabakova (2016), Second Language Acquisition, Chapter 11.

⭐ Overview (for preview) #

  • How information structure (topic/focus) and prosody/word order interact, and why mappings differ across languages.
  • Why pronoun interpretation (null vs. overt, topic continuity/shift) and anaphora resolution are challenging external-interface phenomena.
  • How pragmatic inferences (e.g., scalar implicatures) arise and why they can be delayed or optional in L2 processing.

🎯 Learning goals #

By the end of this week you should be able to:

item.title: Week 11 — L2 Processing & Experimental Methods
item.description:
Week 11 — L2 Processing & Experimental Methods #

Anchor text: Slabakova (2016), Second Language Acquisition, Chapter 12.

⭐ Overview (for preview) #

  • A compact toolkit for studying L2 processing: what offline vs. online methods measure and when to use them.
  • How to align theoretical claims with diagnostic tasks, dependent variables, and analysis plans.
  • Common design pitfalls (speed–accuracy tradeoff, item effects, underpowered samples) and how to avoid them.

🎯 Learning goals #

By the end of this week you should be able to:

item.title: Week 12 — Teaching Implications & the Bottleneck Hypothesis
item.description:
Week 12 — Teaching Implications & the Bottleneck Hypothesis #

Anchor text: Slabakova (2016), Second Language Acquisition, Chapter 13.

⭐ Overview (for preview) #

  • The Bottleneck Hypothesis (BH): why functional morphology (features and their exponents) constitutes the main learning bottleneck in L2, compared to syntax/semantics.
  • Translating theory to pedagogy: which targets are “hard vs. easy,” how to sequence input, and how to design focus-on-form activities that address the bottleneck.
  • Evaluating interventions with compact pre/post designs and diagnostics that align with the hypothesized locus of difficulty.

🎯 Learning goals #

By the end of this week you should be able to:
